extracted.intended_audience: power sector stakeholders (EGU owners/operators), state and Federal regulators, and rulemaking participants/commenters
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and rationale used by EPA in this preamble to identify the Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) for fossil fuel-fired electric generating units, including the evidentiary basis, applicable mitigation technologies (e.g., CCS, natural gas co‑firing, efficient generation), and factors considered in determining feasibility and cost‑effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of scientific assessments to establish need for mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA relies on national and international scientific assessments (e.g., NCA4, NCA5, IPCC) showing observed and projected climate impacts (temperature increases, sea level rise, extreme events, ecosystem losses) to justify the importance of GHG emissions mitigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble cites specific findings (e.g., Arctic nearly sea‑ice free in late summer by mid‑century, coral reef losses, exposure of additional hundreds of millions to extreme heat) and uses these to motivate rulemaking; commenters should rely on or address these assessment findings when discussing the scope/need for standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetization of climate benefits using EPA's FrEDI and social cost of greenhouse gases (SC‑GHGs)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA quantifies climate benefits by monetizing emission reductions through the Framework for Evaluating Damages and Impacts (FrEDI) and application of the social cost of greenhouse gases (SC‑GHGs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FrEDI uses information from over 30 peer‑reviewed impact studies across 20+ impact categories and projects regional physical and economic impacts; EPA did not model avoided temperature change/sea level rise for these specific rules but monetized reductions via SC‑GHGs (see section XII.D). Commenters addressing costs/benefits should consider FrEDI's approach and SC‑GHG inputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER determinations must reflect recent developments, costs, and deployability
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA bases BSER on technologies and practices whose costs have fallen and that are technically and practically deployable across the regulated subcategory (e.g., CCS cost declines, co‑firing availability, high‑efficiency turbines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble explicitly states that lower costs are central to concluding CCS is BSER for certain units; EPA considers technological advances, supportive policies (e.g., IRA tax credits), pilot and FEED progress, and real‑world projects under development or construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carbon capture and storage (CCS) as a BSER technology (components and evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: CCS is characterized as having three major components—CO2 capture, transportation, and sequestration/storage—and the Agency treats CCS as a technology that can be deployed at scale to capture CO2 from EGUs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA cites historical use (solvent capture since 1930s), thousands of miles of CO2 pipelines, tens of millions of tons stored geologically or via EOR, operating projects and many more under development, and specific capture performance targets (e.g., EPA references a 90% capture amine‑based BSER and projects targeting >97% capture). Commenters should address all three CCS components and deployment experience when discussing CCS feasibility or costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: CCS cost and incentive considerations for BSER
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA evaluates recent reductions in CCS costs and the effect of policy incentives (e.g., the IRA's extension/increase of IRC section 45Q tax credits) in determining CCS cost‑effectiveness as BSER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble cites projected 50% fall in CO2 capture costs for coal-fired generation by 2025 (relative to 2010) and notes increases in 45Q (from $50/ton to $85/ton) that materially reduce implementation cost; EPA considers techno‑economic analyses, pilot/FEED results, and industry statements about economics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrated and near‑term project deployment as evidence of feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA uses the existence of operating CCS projects, FEED studies, advanced development projects, pilots, and state policies/mandates (e.g., WY SB42; projects in ND, WV, TX, etc.) as evidence that CCS and other technologies are deployable in the near term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific project examples (Petra Nova, Boundary Dam, Project Tundra, Coal Creek, NET Power Allam‑Fetvedt) and state legislative actions are cited; commenters should reference actual project status, FEED completion, and timelines to support claims about deployability or challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural gas co‑firing as a BSER/mitigation measure for coal steam units
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA recognizes substitution of natural gas for some coal (co‑firing) as a mitigation approach that can be accomplished by modifying existing boilers (installing gas burners, pipeline connections) and notes reduced costs and documented co‑firing at substantial rates for many units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble provides empirical indicators of feasibility: 249 of 565 coal units reported natural gas use in 2021; 29 units co‑fired at ≥60% hourly capacity historically, and more than 80 coal boilers have converted entirely to natural gas since 2011. Commenters should address technical modifications, pipeline availability, historical hourly CO2 emission rates, and capital costs when discussing co‑firing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highly efficient generation for new/reconstructed combustion turbines
rubrics_metrics.description: For new and reconstructed simple‑cycle and combined‑cycle combustion turbines, EPA identifies higher thermal efficiency (plus O&M best practices) as BSER, since better efficiency reduces fuel consumption per MWh and correspondingly lowers CO2 emissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Efficiency improvements for simple‑cycle turbines include higher firing temperatures, increased pressure ratios, intercooling, and other manufacturer innovations; commenters should provide data on demonstrated efficiencies, availability in new builds/reconstructions, and associated emission reductions and costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of unit role, dispatch, and capacity factor in evaluating controls
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA considers the operational role of EGUs (baseload, intermediate, peaking), dispatch order (operating cost driven), capacity factor, and reliability functions (frequency/voltage regulation, black start, reserves) when assessing which units can feasibly and cost‑effectively deploy controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because lower‑cost units run more often, and older plants have more outages, EPA factors in utilization patterns and reliability needs in BSER analyses; commenters should address how proposed controls affect unit availability, capacity factor, grid reliability services, and dispatch economics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of emissions inventories and facility‑level data to target controls
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA relies on the U.S. GHG Inventory and GHGRP facility reporting to identify major stationary GHG sources (e.g., fossil fuel‑fired EGUs dominate the top emitters) and to quantify the contribution of sectors and individual plants when formulating standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble cites specific inventory numbers and GHGRP reporting (e.g., 85 of top 100 large reporting facilities were fossil fuel power plants in 2022); commenters should use or critique these data sources and their representativeness when arguing about scope or stringency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of co‑impacts and non‑climate effects of GHGs
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA notes that some GHGs have impacts beyond climate mediation (e.g., elevated CO2 affects plant growth and ocean acidification; methane contributes to tropospheric ozone; N2O depletes stratospheric ozone) and takes these co‑impacts into account in the broader assessment of harms and benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the primary focus is climate, commenters raising non‑climate harms or benefits (e.g., agricultural/health/ecosystem effects) should provide evidence on those pathways and how the rule's measures would influence them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for sectoral trends, policy drivers, and projections in feasibility judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA incorporates projections (e.g., Power Sector Platform 2023 showing increases in zero‑emitting sources), corporate/state commitments, tax credits, and observed shifts away from coal toward gas and renewables into assessments of what is feasible and cost‑effective for the regulated fleet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble references IRA tax credit structures, state and utility net‑zero and deployment commitments, and projected shares of generation by 2040; commenters should address how these trends affect the marginal cost and availability of compliance options and the likely evolution of the generation mix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational and techno‑economic evidence from pilots, demonstrations, and vendor claims
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA considers vendor and project claims (e.g., Alstom, AEP interviews, NET Power, Linde/BASF techno‑economic studies) as part of the evidentiary record but situates them alongside real deployments, FEED outcomes, and observed cost trajectories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble cites historical optimistic vendor timelines, later cancellations, and more recent advances; commenters should provide transparent data from pilots/FEEDs and be explicit about assumptions and uncertainties in cost/performance claims.
